metadata.title: Walker Jumpman, Extended
metadata.audience: CSYE 7270 reviewers and Walker users extending the starter
metadata.note: Walker-mode walkthrough of walker-jumpman-tharun-m at revision 3aa05bb. Gameplay is native 3840x2160 Godot Movie Maker capture driven through the real Input path; no teleports, no state writes, no disabled collision checks. B00 is an illustrative reconstruction, not a transcript.

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN / walker B00 — ClaudeComposerAsk. Illustrative reconstruction, not a transcript.
beats.narration_text: Hola, this is Liam, in for Bear. Today we play walker jumpman, extended. The starter is Bear's First Steps slice: a small Godot platformer with two gaps, one spike and a finish flag. This build keeps all of that and adds a new character and a new section with a fork in it. The prompt you are looking at is an illustrative reconstruction, not a saved transcript.

props.command: Please use Walker to convert my game design document about a wind-up tin automaton crossing a broken causeway, where the player must choose between a direct spiked terrace and a safe but longer road, into a playable Godot project.
output: CHARACTER  SPROCKET, a wind-up tin automaton
RECONSTRUCTED PROMPT — illustrative, not a transcript

beats.role_note: walker B01 — what was actually built, with a correction. Hesitant writer.
beats.narration_text: Here is what was actually built, and one thing I got wrong on the way. The course goes from nine hundred and sixty pixels to two thousand and eighty, and the flag moves behind the new section, so you cannot finish without playing it. The correction: I sized the first platforms with the textbook jump height, v squared over two g, fifty-three point three pixels. I then measured the real engine. It gives fifty-six. The sixty hertz integrator applies the jump impulse for a full tick before gravity fully bites. Every gap you are about to see was re-sized against the measured number.

props.text:
What was built
   course 960px to 2080px
   flag x=916 to x=1824
   seven new landings, two roads
What I got wrong
   paper: the jump rises 53.3 pixels
   the engine gives 56.0 pixels
   every gap re-sized to that

beats.role_note: CAUSE AND EFFECT — one source change, one visible consequence. Before-frame is a deliberately reconstructed build and is labelled on screen.
beats.narration_text: Here is the trap this starter sets, and the one change that fixes it. The starter builds spike triggers from the level data, but it draws the spikes with the y coordinate hard-coded to the ground line. Two copies of the same geometry, and only one of them reads the data. So put a hazard up on a raised terrace and you get this: the spikes painted on the ground, sixty-four pixels below the trigger SPROCKET is actually walking into. An invisible killer and a decoration that cannot hurt anyone. The fix is one function. Both the trigger builder and the renderer now call it, so they cannot drift apart. Same spot, after.

shot.label: STARTER DRAW CODE + NEW LEVEL DATA

show.event: before: starter draw code against the new level data
after: hazard_triangle() drives both trigger and art

beats.role_note: VERDICT — observed working, versus untested and uncertain.
beats.narration_text: The verdict. Fifty-seven automated checks, zero failures: the starter's twenty-five mechanics checks, its nine keyboard checks byte-identical, and twenty-three new ones. What is uncertain is smaller but real. The terrace jump has eight pixels of margin. I predicted a first-timer would bonk the underside before the painted guide taught the timing, and when the level was actually played, that did not happen. That prediction is marked refuted in the change brief rather than deleted. But one person played it, and it was the person who placed the platforms and already knew where the window was. That is the weakest sample there is.

beats.role_note: YOUR TURN — one concrete experiment. Liam signs off here.
beats.narration_text: Your turn. The next improvement is the limitation I can name most precisely. That painted launch guide is positioned by hand. Move the terrace and forget to move the paint, and the picture disagrees with the physics again, which is exactly the bug this build fixed everywhere else. So compute the guide from the measured take-off window at load time, the way the spikes already derive their shape. Then play it, take the low road first, and tell me whether doubling back reads as a decision or just as getting lost. Liam, in for Bear.

props.command: Derive the launch-guide band from the measured take-off window at load time, so the paint and the physics cannot disagree.
output: the guide is the last hand-placed number in the level
every other marker is derived from level data
hazard_triangle() already proves the pattern works
